chapter.title: The Python Standard Library
chapter.para: Python comes with a large library, and every module of it is a .py~import away. These recipes use a few of the most common; each shows, besides the module, one thing about the bridge worth knowing.

section.title: JSON
section.para: You want to write and read JSON.

How it works. .py~dict(.py~kw(...)) makes a dict from keyword arguments, as Python's dict(a=1) does. The value for "oo" is boxed as a bool: a Rexx 1 would go as the number 1, and JSON would say 1, not true. What loads returns is Python's: a dict, whose "langs" is a list, indexed from 0, and iterated with DO OVER.

section.title: CSV
section.para: You want to read and write CSV.

How it works. Each row of a DictReader is a dict. Its values are Python strings, which come to Rexx as Rexx strings, so row["score"] + 5 is Rexx's addition. io~StringIO~new makes an in-memory file: io~StringIO alone is the class, since classes are not called without new or arguments. A Rexx Array is a row to write. Python's csv ends its lines with carriage return and line feed, which the sample strips.

section.title: Statistics
section.para: You want the mean, the median and the standard deviation of some numbers.
How it works. The Rexx Array goes as a list of ints. The results are Python's: the mean of integers that comes out whole is an int, 5, and the standard deviation a float, 2.0.

section.title: An SQL Database
section.para: You want SQL, without a database server.

How it works. sqlite3 comes with Python; ":memory:" is a database that lives while the connection does. The rows to insert are a Rexx Array of Arrays, a list of lists to Python, which fills the ? placeholders. The rows a query returns are tuples: row[0] is the first column.

section.title: Dates
section.para: How it works. Rexx's operators on a Python object are Python's: d + dt~timedelta(...) adds thirty days, and the difference of two dates is a timedelta, whose days is a number.

section.title: Random Numbers
section.para: You want random numbers, the same on every run.
How it works. random~seed(2026) seeds the generator with the number 2026, by the number rule: the text "2026" would seed it differently. choice picks from a Rexx Array, which goes as a list.

section.title: UUIDs
section.para: How it works. uuid~NAMESPACE_DNS finds the constant: no other name of the module matches it. uuid~uuid4, a function without arguments, is called. A UUID is a Python object, which SAY shows as Python's str does; its string is that text.

section.title: URLs
section.para: You want the parts of a URL, or to make a query string.
How it works. .py~import("urllib.parse") returns the submodule parse itself. urlparse returns a named tuple, whose fields are its attributes.

section.title: Logging
section.para: You want Python's logging, here into a string.

How it works. The module has both logging.info, a function, and logging.INFO, a constant. Rexx's INFO matches both, and the lowercase one wins, so logging~INFO would call the function. The constant needs its exact name: logging~getattr("INFO"). What getvalue returns is a Python string, so a Rexx string, split into lines with Rexx's makeArray.
